newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle docks at Russia's Mir space station.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle docks at Russia's Mir space station.

text.p: The U.S. shuttle Atlantis docked at Russia's Mir space station on Tuesday night, bringing fresh supplies and a change of crew for the orbiting outpost.
The two craft linked up at 10:54 p.m. EST (0354 GMT) as they soared about 250 miles (400 km) above Russia, southeast of Moscow. It was the fifth time Atlantis has visited the station.
"Contact and capture," radioed shuttle commander Mike Baker as the spaceship's petal-like docking rings came together.

Electric motors then drew the two craft together, completing the docking process and making an air-tight seal. The hatches between the station and the shuttle were due to swing open at 12:41 a.m. EST (0541 GMT).
Mir's current U.S. resident, John Blaha, his face pressed against a window of Mir, watched the arrival of Atlantis, which was to take him home after a 128-day mission.
"We see someone in the window of Mir with their thumb out," Baker reported after successfully completing the docking.
Baker, making his fourth space flight, had carefully flown past the station's forest of delicate, electricity-generating solar panels as he inched Atlantis toward the docking port.
Astronaut Jerry Linenger is to take Blaha's place on Mir. The 41-year-old astronaut, a Navy captain and medical doctor, was to spend four months aboard the station.
His tour of duty is scheduled to end in May, a month before the birth of his second child is expected. The astronaut has accepted that a shuttle delay could make him miss the birth.
Atlantis and Mir were to remain locked together for five days while the two crews moved a total of 5,975 lbs (2,710 kg) of supplies and equipment between the craft.
Russian space officials admitted before Atlantis' launch that their cash-strapped space programme now relies on the shuttle to ferry supplies and equipment to the Russian station.
Linenger will be the fourth U.S. astronaut to live aboard Mir as NASA learns to work with Russia before embarking on the international space station project later this year.

"It is incredible that once two great superpowers who were enemies with nuclear missiles aimed at each other are now holding hands," Blaha told NASA Administrator Daniel Goldin on Tuesday in a telephone call from Mir.
"That's even way beyond science, NASA and space flight as far as the impact that can have on world peace."
Blaha said he had not missed anything while he was away from earth apart from his wife of 30 years, Brenda.
"I missed my wife," he said. "I hadn't realised how much the separation would hit me."
Blaha, an avid football fan, will be back on earth in time for the Super Bowl on Jan. 26, although his team, the Dallas Cowboys, will not be playing.
